author: ezgi-gizem-berkay
description: In less than a day, Vesuvius wiped out a Roman city of 15,000 people under meters of pumice and ash. A violent earthquake had warned them seventeen years earlier.

hero.hook: A roar as if the sky were splitting open, then stones falling before anyone understood: Pompeii had eighteen hours left to live.

blocks.text: A roar, as if the sky were splitting open. Stones falling before anyone understood what was happening, roofs giving way like paper, a cloud of ash swallowing the daylight. Nearly **2,000 years** ago, a bustling Roman city on the shores of the Mediterranean was buried in silence by the eruption of [[Vesuvius]].

[[Campania]], bathed by the calm waters of the Gulf of Naples, had long drawn poets, travelers and emperors. Its climate and fertile soil allowed **three harvests a year** and precious crops, vines and olive trees. The Greek geographer [[Strabo]] and a few high-ranking Romans knew that this wealth came from the mountain's volcanic past. Yet nobody expected a catastrophe.

Pompeii lies about **240 kilometers** south of Rome, on a plateau overlooking the Sarno Valley. Around AD 79, the town had some **15,000 inhabitants**. It lived on trade: wine, woolen garments and above all [[garum]], a fermented fish sauce.

blocks.caption: The Via dell'Abbondanza in Pompeii: raised stepping stones and ruts worn by cart wheels.

blocks.text: Vesuvius, for its part, remains one of the most famous volcanoes in the world, and millions of people live in its shadow today. Since Roman times it has erupted at least **50 times**, mostly on a small scale. In AD 79, it buried Pompeii under several meters of [[pumice]] and ash. Forgotten for nearly **1,500 years**, the town is now one of the best-preserved sites of antiquity, precisely because of the volcanic layer that protected it.

sections.title: A prosperous city at the foot of Vesuvius

blocks.text: On **October 24**, AD 79, at around 1 pm, the mountain exploded. Vesuvius released thermal energy comparable to **100,000 Hiroshima bombs** and drove a column of pumice and ash more than **32 kilometers** into the sky. For twelve hours, a rain of stones fell on the town.

blocks.caption: The Last Day of Pompeii, by Karl Bryullov (1833): the crowd flees under the rain of stones.

blocks.text: For centuries the eruption was dated August 24, AD 79. A charcoal inscription discovered in the town in **2018** moved the date to October 24.

During this first phase, pumice piled up on the roofs, which gave way and crushed those sheltering inside. At its peak, the volcano spat out nearly **100,000 tons** of magma per second, and the whole region sank into total darkness. Then the column collapsed, and a [[pyroclastic current]], a scorching flow of gas and ash, surged toward the town. The eruption produced **six such waves**; the fourth and fifth struck Pompeii. In about eighteen hours, the entire city was buried.

sections.title: October 24, AD 79: the rain of pumice

blocks.text: The first current to reach the town was the fourth wave, at around **7 am**. The city walls only partly held it back, and it poured into the streets and houses. Those who had survived the rain of stones and stayed behind died almost instantly, hit by a thermal shock of **250 to 300 °C**. But most of the inhabitants had already fled: the currents killed those who remained, not the whole town.

For Pompeii was no ordinary settlement. It had its own forum, its bathhouses and **two theaters**. Its inns and taverns, the tabernae, served merchants arriving by land and by sea. Its many bakeries point to a strong demand for bread.
Pompeii's amphitheater was built about **150 years** before the Colosseum in Rome. It could hold up to **20,000 spectators** for gladiator fights and wild-beast hunts, the venationes.

sections.title: The burning cloud strikes a town like no other

blocks.text: As soon as the excavations began, Pompeii's fame spread around the world. Its art and architecture left a lasting mark on how Europe pictured classical antiquity, and archaeologists are still at work there. The most striking finds are the **plaster casts**: plaster is poured into the cavities left by decayed bodies. The heat of the eruption fixed their contorted postures, and these human figures bring the tragedy to light with brutal realism.

blocks.caption: The casts of the victims in the Garden of the Fugitives, Pompeii.

blocks.text: Yet the tremors were nothing new. Seventeen years earlier, in **AD 62** (or 63), a violent earthquake had badly damaged the city, which was still under repair when Vesuvius woke up. Rather than reading it as a warning, the residents saw ordinary tremors and went on living as before. The death toll is usually put at around **2,000**, although the bodies identified so far number about **1,500**, and estimates vary.

events.detail: The town is still a building site seventeen years later.

events.title: The date corrected

blocks.text: On October 24, AD 79, a rain of pumice and then two burning clouds erased in eighteen hours a city of 15,000 people that had mistaken its earthquakes for ordinary tremors.
